title: Nanofabricated ultraflexible electrodes for chronic, high-density neural recording and stimulation
authors: Weinan Wang, Yuhang Ma, Pavlo Zolotavin, Liuyang Sun, Hanqing Wang, Kyu Hyun Lee, Kalman A. Katlowitz, Carter A. Kelly, Hanlin Zhu, Rongkang Yin, Yingchu Sun, Robin Kim, Luis De La Palma Piedras, Jiaao Zhang, Yuxuan Liu, Xiaorong Zhang, Elizabeth A. Mickiewicz, Philip Adenekan, Nicole R. Provenza, Ganesh Rao, Alla Y. Karpova, Benjamin Y. Hayden, Sameer A. Sheth, Loren M. Frank, Lan Luan, Chong Xie
summary: Nanofabrication increases channel density while preserving small, ultraflexible neural probes.
introduction: We use electron-beam lithography to pattern dense interconnects on flexible polymer probes for chronic recording and stimulation.

cover.title: Inside an ultraflexible electrode
cover.alt: Exploded schematic showing two interconnect layers between insulating layers, with magnified insets of contacts, wiring, and openings.
cover.caption: Three polyimide insulation layers separate two levels of metal interconnects. The insets show how these traces reach the contact layer and how openings in the encapsulation expose individual electrode sites.

sections.title: Probe architecture and footprint
sections.description: Electron-beam lithography fits more independently addressed sites onto a slender polymer shank. The layer structure and probe comparison show how the device achieves this density.

figures.title: Inside an ultraflexible electrode
figures.alt: Exploded schematic showing two interconnect layers between insulating layers, with magnified insets of contacts, wiring, and openings.
figures.caption: Three polyimide insulation layers separate two levels of metal interconnects. The insets show how these traces reach the contact layer and how openings in the encapsulation expose individual electrode sites.

figures.title: Channel count and tissue footprint
figures.alt: Log–log plot of simultaneous channels per shank versus cross-sectional area per electrode.
figures.caption: The red star marks EBL-NETs. Moving up the plot means more simultaneous recording channels per shank. Moving left means a smaller cross-section per electrode. The comparison includes Utah arrays, conventional and EBL silicon shanks, Neuropixels, carbon fibers, planar polymer electrodes, and photolithographic NETs.

sections.title: From the probe to a metal trace
sections.description: Across three shank designs, the same contact, via, and trace geometry links each recording site to its own lead.

figures.title: Three probe lengths, one wiring strategy
figures.alt: Three probes on the left. On the right, a contact micrograph, a wiring schematic, and a scanning electron micrograph show progressively finer details.
figures.caption: From left to right, the 128-, 384-, and 512-channel probes have contact coverage of 2, 5, and 5 mm and implantable lengths of 5–7, 10, and 5.5 mm, respectively (scale bar 1 mm). At upper right, 15 µm circular contacts connect through 5 µm vias (scale bar 50 µm). The schematic shows individual gray traces reaching contacts through black vias in orange polyimide. The electron micrograph resolves 150 nm metal lines separated by 150 nm gaps (scale bar 1 µm).

sections.title: Recording and tracking single neurons
sections.description: Densely spaced contacts sample the spatial signature of each spike. Repeated recordings show how those signatures and spike timing evolve across days.

figures.title: Locating single neurons along a shank
figures.alt: High-pass traces beside a map of estimated single-unit positions and two magnified regions showing extracellular waveforms.
figures.caption: A 128-channel EBL-NET records high-pass filtered extracellular signals (left). Black dots in the center mark contacts. Each color identifies a sorted unit, and circle size encodes spike amplitude. Two enlarged regions show mean spike waveforms across neighboring contacts and the estimated unit positions. Recording data from Hanqing Wang.

figures.title: Tracking five units across ten days
figures.alt: Ten days of color-coded mean waveforms for five units, shown on adjacent recording contacts.
figures.caption: For each of five tracked units, the same group of contacts is shown across ten days. Colors distinguish recording days. The waveform scale bars are 50 µV and 1 ms. Recording data from Yuhang Ma.

figures.title: Spike timing across sessions
figures.alt: Ten daily interspike-interval histograms for each of two tracked units.
figures.caption: For units i and iv in the waveform comparison, each histogram shows the fraction of successive spikes separated by a given interval. The ten daily distributions provide a second view of each unit’s stability. Recording data from Yuhang Ma.

heading: Parallel implantation of flexible neural electrodes
title: Centimani: An implantation robot enabling parallel, distributed implantation of flexible electrode arrays for large-scale bi-directional neural interface
summary: A precision robot implants flexible neural threads in parallel across distributed targets.
introduction: Centimani brings together independent positioning, optical targeting, and parallel insertion to place flexible electrode arrays across multiple brain regions. Weinan Wang built the robot in collaboration with Yu Wu, Romain Albouy, and Curtis Chen.

cover.title: Thirty-two independently positioned needles
cover.caption: Thirty-two XYZ piezoelectric stages form a 4 × 8 array. A beamsplitter and zoom microscope bring the needle tips and cortical surface into one view. The close-ups show the needle array and how a needle engages a flexible thread. Weinan Wang built the robot in collaboration with Yu Wu, Romain Albouy, and Curtis Chen.

sections.title: Positioning and delivering 32 threads
sections.description: A portable cartridge couples the flexible array to the robot. Each needle can move independently before the threads advance together.

figures.title: Thirty-two independently positioned needles
figures.caption: Thirty-two XYZ piezoelectric stages form a 4 × 8 array. A beamsplitter and zoom microscope bring the needle tips and cortical surface into one view. The close-ups show the needle array and how a needle engages a flexible thread. Weinan Wang built the robot in collaboration with Yu Wu, Romain Albouy, and Curtis Chen.
figures.alt: Thirty-two independently positioned needles

figures.title: Where the needles can reach
figures.caption: The array spans 3.5–13.5 mm in width and 1.5–11.5 mm in length. Minimum inter-needle spacing is 500 µm, with insertion depths from 0 to 10 mm.
figures.alt: Where the needles can reach

figures.title: From cartridge to implanted array
figures.caption: The assembled 32-thread cartridge is positioned as a 4 × 8 array before targeting. Microscopy shows the threads after insertion into hydrogel, with a magnified detail. Microcomputed tomography reconstructs their three-dimensional arrangement.
figures.alt: From cartridge to implanted array

sections.title: Optical targeting and placement
sections.description: An optical overlay guides lateral positioning. Separate height adjustments account for the curvature of the cortical surface.

figures.title: Choosing cortical entry sites
figures.caption: A 50/50 beamsplitter overlays the microneedle tips and cortical surface. The operator selects entry sites on the cortical image. The XY stages move each needle from its initial position to its designated target.
figures.alt: Choosing cortical entry sites

figures.title: Following the cortical surface
figures.caption: The array is positioned above the exposed cortex. Four corner touchdown measurements and a model of the cortical surface set the individual height adjustments. After the needles withdraw, the flexible threads remain at their insertion sites.
figures.alt: Following the cortical surface

figures.title: Measuring targeting error
figures.caption: Dyed needle tips marked a clay surface at the selected targets. The scatterplot and marginal box plots report horizontal and vertical offsets between intended and observed sites across 168 paired measurements.
figures.alt: Measuring targeting error

sections.title: Recording across regions
sections.description: Contact maps locate the recordings. The traces, unit metrics, and cross-correlations describe what the distributed array measured.

figures.title: Coverage across animals and recording sites
figures.caption: Estimated contact positions are shown for five mice. In a baseline recording from LSNET17, the local field potential is mapped across the array as a z-score. The final view distinguishes contacts with detected units from the remaining registered contacts.
figures.alt: Coverage across animals and recording sites

figures.title: Signals across shanks and cortical regions
figures.caption: Local field potentials and spike-band recordings are grouped by shank and anatomical region in LSNET17. Example unit waveforms appear beside the corresponding channels. The scale bars indicate the different amplitudes and timescales of the three signal views.
figures.alt: Signals across shanks and cortical regions

figures.title: Unit quality and yield
figures.caption: The distributions summarize spike amplitude, firing rate, signal-to-noise ratio, and intervals shorter than 2 ms. Across one 20-minute baseline recording per mouse, 1,208 curated units were found on 1,455 usable channels. Of these, 1,007 met the single-unit criterion of fewer than 2% of intervals below 2 ms.
figures.alt: Unit quality and yield

figures.title: Putative monosynaptic connections
figures.caption: The cross-correlogram for LSNET19 units 178 and 40 peaks at a lag of 2 ms. The directional matrix summarizes 53 units, with red for putative excitatory links and blue for inhibitory links. The anatomical view joins the recording contacts assigned to each pair.
figures.alt: Putative monosynaptic connections

sections.title: Mapping responses to stimulation
sections.description: Single-contact stimulation links pulse timing and unit responses to the anatomy of the distributed interface.

figures.title: One site, two example responses
figures.caption: A 3 µA pulse train at stimulation channel 30 is shown alongside the recorded trace. The pulse inset gives phase timing, and colored markers identify spikes assigned to example units 12 and 13.
figures.alt: One site, two example responses

figures.title: Pulse-aligned responses
figures.caption: The three-dimensional view places the stimulated and responding contacts in the brain. The blue and orange waveforms identify the two example units. For unit 12, the raster and peristimulus histogram align spikes to stimulation onset to show the timing of the response.
figures.alt: Pulse-aligned responses

figures.title: Responses by site and unit
figures.caption: Each small raster shows repeated trials for a stimulation channel and a recorded unit at the site’s threshold current. Grouping channels and units by cortical region reveals the distribution of responses across the array.
figures.alt: Responses by site and unit

figures.title: Train-responsive site–unit pairs
figures.caption: The matrix maps 291 train-responsive pairs across 77 stimulation sites and 123 units. Black entries mark responsive pairs, grouped by cortical region and hemisphere. The circular plot shows the threshold-current connections by cortical region.
figures.alt: Train-responsive site–unit pairs

figures.title: Anatomical distribution of responses
figures.caption: The brain view connects stimulation sites to responding recording contacts. Including pulse-locked responses, the map contains 317 site–unit responses across 77 stimulation sites and 107 recording contacts. The inset enlarges a group of contacts and their connections.
figures.alt: Anatomical distribution of responses

title: Ultraflexible probes with a custom ASIC for 512-channel recording and 128-channel stimulation
authors: Weinan Wang, Gerald Topalli, Xiaorong Zhang, Jiyuan Duan, Yiling Xie, Pavlo Zolotavin, Howard Wang, Lan Luan, Taiyun Chi, and Chong Xie
summary: A custom ASIC integrates high-channel-count recording and programmable stimulation with an ultraflexible probe array.
introduction: Four ultraflexible shanks connect to a custom ASIC that records neural activity and delivers programmable current pulses. Bench measurements characterize the hardware, and two in-vivo recordings show how the system resolves single units and measures their responses to stimulation. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.

cover.title: An ultraflexible probe bonded to the headstage
cover.caption: The four-shank array connects to a custom ASIC with 512 recording and 128 stimulation channels. The recording pixels occupy 8 × 7 mm of the 9 × 15 mm chip. The 2 mm, 500 µm and 100 µm scale bars distinguish the assembly, four-shank spacing and single-shank detail. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
cover.alt: Photograph of the headstage with magnified views of four shanks and an individual shank.

sections.title: Probe and headstage
sections.description: Four shanks share one recording and stimulation interface. The photographs show the bonded device at three scales.

figures.title: An ultraflexible probe bonded to the headstage
figures.caption: The four-shank array connects to a custom ASIC with 512 recording and 128 stimulation channels. The recording pixels occupy 8 × 7 mm of the 9 × 15 mm chip. The 2 mm, 500 µm and 100 µm scale bars distinguish the assembly, four-shank spacing and single-shank detail. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Photograph of the headstage with magnified views of four shanks and an individual shank.

figures.title: A 1.2 g packaged headstage
figures.caption: The conceptual rendering, based on device photographs, shows the packaged headstage in position and illustrates the two signal paths for recording neural activity and delivering stimulation. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: A headstage on a mouse with recording and stimulation signal diagrams.

sections.title: Bench measurements
sections.description: Saline recordings characterize noise with the probe attached. The electrical specifications and cross-platform comparison put the measurement in context.

figures.title: Recording and stimulation specifications
figures.caption: Each recording channel samples at 31.25 kS/s with a 12-bit ADC and consumes 17.24 µW. Monopolar or bipolar stimulation spans 1.5–22.5 µA in 1.5 µA steps, with ±10 V compliance. The table gives the remaining electrical and timing limits. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Electrical specifications for the recording front end, converter and programmable stimulator.

figures.title: Noise with the probe attached
figures.caption: With the four-shank probe in saline, input-referred noise was 6.34 ± 0.64 µV RMS over 1 Hz–10 kHz. The histogram contains 465 measurements in the supplied range. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Saline measurement schematic and a histogram of input-referred noise.

figures.title: Comparing recording ASICs
figures.caption: The comparison covers Intan RHD2164, Neuralink, Neuropixels 2.0 and GChip. For GChip, the reported 4 and 7 µV RMS values were measured without and with a probe, respectively, over 1 Hz–10 kHz. Noise bandwidth and area definitions vary by design. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Comparison of channel count, noise, bandwidth, power and area per channel across four designs.

sections.title: Recording single units
sections.description: The October 16 recording links signals across channels to spatially localized units and measures of isolation quality.

figures.title: Spike-band activity across three shanks
figures.caption: A 120 ms window shows simultaneous spike-band traces on Sh0, Sh1 and Sh2. Channel numbers indicate row positions on Sh0. Dashed rows mark unavailable channels. The scale bars indicate 20 ms and 1 mV. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Vertically aligned spike-band traces across three shanks, with common time and voltage scales.

figures.title: Localizing units along the probe
figures.caption: The recording yielded 292 curated units across three shanks (85, 107 and 100 on Sh0, Sh1 and Sh2). The boxed Sh1 region contains 22 units. Mean templates from 19 meet the channel-display threshold and appear in the enlarged footprint. Scale bars indicate 100 µm, 1 ms and 100 µV. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Unit locations along three shanks beside an enlarged spatial footprint of mean waveforms on Sh1.

figures.title: Assessing unit quality
figures.caption: The distributions show spike amplitude, template peak-to-peak voltage, signal-to-noise ratio and the percentage of interspike intervals shorter than 2 ms. Of 292 curated units, 279 fall below the dashed 1% short-interval threshold. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Four histograms showing amplitudes, signal quality and short interspike intervals.

sections.title: Responses to stimulation
sections.description: The October 19 recording follows stimulation from the selected contact to the response of nearby units.

figures.title: Stimulating and recording across shanks
figures.caption: Three sites on Sh0 and Sh2 delivered stimulation while nearby contacts recorded on all three shanks. Circle size denotes template peak-to-peak amplitude and filled circles identify units with nominal rate increases. Enlarged neighborhoods show median waveforms and the five Sh1 contacts used below. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Three shank maps with stimulation stars, local waveform footprints and five numbered recording contacts.

figures.title: Responses at each stimulation site
figures.caption: Each column shows trains delivered to one stimulation site, with one row per train in each unit block. The 29 units comprise 9 on Sh0, 15 on Sh1 and 5 on Sh2. Shading marks nominal rate changes across 87 unit–site tests (paired bootstrap p < 0.05 and |d| > 0.5). Eight units showed a nominal rate increase. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Raster plots aligned to stimulation at three sites for 29 units.

figures.title: The programmed biphasic pulse
figures.caption: Each cathodic-leading pulse used −6 and +6 µA phases of 150 µs separated by 60 µs. Ten pulses at 50 Hz formed one train, with 20 trains delivered per site. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: A cathodic-first, charge-balanced pulse with equal 150 µs phases and a 60 µs gap.

figures.title: Signals during one stimulation train
figures.caption: At stimulation site 3, the top trace shows the baseline-subtracted raw signal at Sh1 chip channel 90. Below it are five processed signals from the numbered Sh1 contacts, followed by color-coded unit events. Time is aligned to train onset. Gerald Topalli of Taiyun Chi's lab developed the GChip ASIC.
figures.alt: Baseline-subtracted raw trace, five contact traces and unit event times during stimulation.
